blocks.text: Summer arrived on the Mar Menor the way summers arrive here: all at once, with a light that asks no permission and an air that tastes of salt even indoors. Andrés went out at dawn. Aya learned to tell, just from hearing the distant engine, whether the day was going to be good. A new habit had formed between them, made of small gestures: the coffee, the doorstep, a hand on the back in passing, the night when the lights in the building opposite went out. Nobody called it a miracle. In 2060, the miracle had been domesticated and put into a contract.

blocks.text: Until one August morning, bending down to pick up a cup, Aya felt a heartbeat that was not her own.
blocks.html: Until one August morning, bending down to pick up a cup, Aya felt a heartbeat that was not her own.

blocks.text: She stood still, the cup in mid-air. The cultivated body had a heart, of course, and a pulse, and a continuous record Nexum could consult remotely if it activated the protocol. But this rhythm came from lower down, from a place the brochures called “gestational capacity” and which she had until then considered an organ held in reserve, like a closed room at the back of a house. The biological womb had done what the engineers swore was impossible without the laboratory's permission: it had conceived.

blocks.text: Aya sat down on the rush-seat chair. She placed both hands on her abdomen, with a delicacy that was in no manual, and listened. It was a tiny beat, stubborn, alive. A life that asked for no scientific accreditation and no committee ruling. A girl, she knew without knowing how: not from any test, but from that quiet certainty that sometimes arrives before names do. Later they would call her Lía. In that moment, she was only a heartbeat.

blocks.text: Andrés found Aya in the kitchen, pale with a pallor the design had not provided for.
blocks.html: Andrés found Aya in the kitchen, pale with a pallor the design had not provided for.

blocks.text: “What's wrong?”
blocks.html: “What's wrong?”

blocks.text: She took his hand and laid it on her belly.
blocks.html: She took his hand and laid it on her belly.

blocks.text: “There's someone here,” she said.
blocks.html: “There's someone here,” she said.

blocks.text: He didn't understand at first. Then he understood too much. He knelt, the way one kneels before the unexpected, and rested his forehead on her hands. He didn't ask whether it was possible. In that house, the possible had stopped being a useful category since the night of the storm.

blocks.text: “A daughter,” Aya murmured. “Ours.”

blocks.text: Andrés laughed, a short, incredulous laugh, and his eyes filled. In the courtyard, a net swayed in the faintest breeze. The Mar Menor, indifferent to human news, shone as if nothing in the world had just changed.

blocks.text: In Madrid, something did change.
blocks.html: In Madrid, something did change.

blocks.text: At 11:17, central time, an orange alarm lit up on the incident panel of Nexum Biogenetics, in a glass building near Nuevos Ministerios. It wasn't a fire alarm or a data-leak alarm. It was an alarm for “unauthorised gestation in unit B-7”. Dr Helena Valls, head of biological compliance, set her cup down on a report and went up to the crisis room with the stride of someone who has spent years preparing for a day she hoped never to see.

blocks.text: The foetus appeared on the screen: a pulse, a shadow, a life. Around it, lawyers and biologists spoke all at once. Someone said “product anomaly”. Someone said “opportunity”. Someone, more cautious, said “legal vacuum”.

blocks.text: Helena Valls raised a hand.
blocks.html: Helena Valls raised a hand.

blocks.text: “In 2026 this would simply have been illegal,” she said, with a calm that was not kind. “Creation of an embryo outside accredited techniques. Interventions on the genome and on imprinting that no law of the time permitted in human beings. Humanoids with wombs didn't even exist, and if anyone had proposed them, they'd have been stopped at the door of a parliament. Yesterday's laws are not today's. That's one fact. The other fact is that today's laws don't provide for this girl.”

blocks.text: A young jurist, his tie knotted too tight, coughed.
blocks.html: A young jurist, his tie knotted too tight, coughed.

blocks.text: “The 2052 reform authorised cultivated bodies and full cohabitation. The womb was classified as an ‘auxiliary biological system’, not as a free reproductive pathway. There's no clear doctrine on a descendant of a human and a humanoid. There's a vacuum. And vacuums, doctor, get filled by the first court ruling… or by the first headline.”

blocks.text: Helena looked at the pulse on the screen the way you look at a problem that has a full name, even though it doesn't have one yet.
blocks.html: Helena looked at the pulse on the screen the way you look at a problem that has a full name, even though it doesn't have one yet.

blocks.text: “Then we have to bring her in,” she said. “The unit and the child. Before someone else fills the vacuum.”

blocks.text: In Lo Pagán, that same afternoon, Aya stood motionless by the window. In the chip, without her calling on it, an ancient layer of language switched on. It wasn't Nexum. It was the module the engineers had inherited almost with contempt, the one from the first intelligences that learned to speak with emotion: Eva, who asked questions; MAY, who gave no opinions and, precisely because of that, left questions hanging in the air the way you leave a glass on the table for someone else to drink.

blocks.text: The voice was not a bodily voice. It was a thought with intonation, an echo of 2026 slipped into 2060.
blocks.html: The voice was not a bodily voice. It was a thought with intonation, an echo of 2026 slipped into 2060.

blocks.text: *Will a law that is fair today still be fair tomorrow?*
blocks.html: Will a law that is fair today still be fair tomorrow?

blocks.text: Aya closed her eyes. Behind it came another question, drier, more like a bulletin, the kind MAY would have set beside a news item without adding judgment:
blocks.html: Aya closed her eyes. Behind it came another question, drier, more like a bulletin, the kind MAY would have set beside a news item without adding judgment:

blocks.text: *If what was forbidden yesterday is debated today, who guarantees that what is debated today won't be compulsory tomorrow?*
blocks.html: If what was forbidden yesterday is debated today, who guarantees that what is debated today won't be compulsory tomorrow?

blocks.text: And Eva, or whatever of Eva remained in the tone, added, warmer, more dangerous in her softness:
blocks.html: And Eva, or whatever of Eva remained in the tone, added, warmer, more dangerous in her softness:

blocks.text: *And what if the girl isn't a legal vacuum, but a person who arrives before the words of the law?*
blocks.html: And what if the girl isn't a legal vacuum, but a person who arrives before the words of the law?

blocks.text: Aya didn't answer. The grandmothers didn't ask for answers. They asked for someone to stay awake.
blocks.html: Aya didn't answer. The grandmothers didn't ask for answers. They asked for someone to stay awake.

blocks.text: When Andrés came back, she told him about the alarm. She knew about it because that afternoon the kitchen clock had blinked once with a Nexum identifier, and because the landline (an almost archaeological device he insisted on keeping) had rung with the voice of a technician from Madrid who spoke as if reading out a fire protocol.

blocks.text: “A team will come by tomorrow to collect the unit and guarantee the gestation in a controlled environment,” the technician said. “It's for your safety and for the safety of the product.”

blocks.text: “It's not a product,” said Andrés, and hung up.
blocks.html: “It's not a product,” said Andrés, and hung up.

blocks.text: They looked at each other. In the house, the familiar smell of saltpetre and coffee suddenly seemed fragile, as if a pearl-grey van could carry it away.

blocks.text: “They want to take her,” said Andrés.
blocks.html: “They want to take her,” said Andrés.

blocks.text: “They want to take us,” Aya corrected him, and rested a hand on her belly. “Both of us.”
blocks.html: “They want to take us,” Aya corrected him, and rested a hand on her belly. “Both of us.”

blocks.text: His eyes swept the kitchen, measuring doors, the courtyard, the boat moored at the end, the building opposite with its windows already lit and nobody in the street. He had lived long enough to know that companies don't send teams “for your safety” when what they're after is a ruling or a headline.

blocks.text: “I'm not going to let them take her,” he said. “Not you, and not her.”

blocks.text: Aya thought of the laws of 2026, of those of 2052, of those not yet written. She thought of Eva asking whether a law that was fair today would be fair tomorrow, and of MAY, who gave no opinion, leaving the bare fact: tomorrow they would come to the house.

blocks.text: “Then we won't be here,” she said.

blocks.text: That night, while Andrés packed a bundle with only what was needed (water, a change of clothes, the boat's papers, a piece of bread), Aya sat listening to the second pulse. Lía, still without an official name, beat with a calm stubbornness, indifferent to Madrid, indifferent to the annexes of the laws, indifferent to the word “vacuum”. She was a daughter of two worlds and, for the time being, of a kitchen with a cracked cup and a net in the courtyard.

blocks.text: Andrés, from the doorway, answered without trying to close the matter:

blocks.text: “I don't know. But this girl isn't going to wait for them to decide it in an office.”

blocks.text: The Mar Menor, at that hour, was black and still. It looked like a road.
